habsburg-dynasty.s: The Habsburg dynasty was one of Europe's leading royal houses, ruling Austria for centuries and holding the title of Holy Roman Emperor almost continuously from the fifteenth century. A Spanish branch ruled the Spanish Empire in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

hacienda.s: A hacienda was a large landed estate in Spanish America, typically producing livestock or crops and relying on dependent or indebted labour. Haciendas became dominant economic and social units in the colonial countryside.

hadith.s: Hadith are reports of the sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad, transmitted through chains of narrators. Together with the Quran they form a principal source of Islamic law and practice.

hafsid-dynasty.s: The Hafsid dynasty ruled Ifriqiya, centred on Tunis, from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century. It began with Almohad governors of the region who later declared independence.

hagia-sophia.s: The Hagia Sophia is a great domed church in Constantinople completed in 537 CE under the emperor Justinian I. For centuries it was the cathedral of the Byzantine Empire and one of the largest buildings in the world.

haiku.s: Haiku is a short form of Japanese poetry, traditionally of three phrases following a five-seven-five syllable pattern and often evoking nature and the seasons. The form was developed by poets such as Matsuo Bashō during the Edo period.

haile-selassie.s: Haile Selassie was the last Emperor of Ethiopia, who died in 1975. He went into exile after the Italian invasion of 1935 and was restored in 1941 when the Italian Empire's East African holdings collapsed.

haiti.s: Haiti is a Caribbean country that occupies the western part of the island of Hispaniola, formerly the French colony of Saint-Domingue. Many of its enslaved population came from West Africa, including Yoruba people from the region of the Oyo Empire.

haitian-revolution.s: The Haitian Revolution of 1791–1804 was an uprising of enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue that led to the abolition of slavery there and the creation of the independent state of Haiti. It was the only successful large-scale slave revolt to found a state.

haitian-vodou.s: Haitian Vodou is an Afro-Caribbean religion that developed in Haiti among enslaved Africans and their descendants, combining West and Central African traditions with elements of Catholicism. It incorporates spirits and practices with roots in Yoruba and Fon religion.

hajj.s: The hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca that every Muslim who is able is expected to make at least once in a lifetime, one of the five pillars of Islam. Pilgrimage routes linked West Africa and the Sahel to the Hejaz.

hakura.s: The hakura was a land-grant system of the Darfur Sultanate, introduced under its founder Sulayman Solong, in which the sultan granted territorial rights in exchange for loyalty, service, revenue and military levies. It bound diverse communities to the throne and structured…

hall-of-mirrors.s: The Hall of Mirrors is the grand gallery of the Palace of Versailles near Paris, built under Louis XIV. In January 1871, during the Franco-Prussian War, King Wilhelm I of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor there.

halland.s: Halland is a province on the west coast of present-day Sweden, formerly held by Denmark. It passed to Sweden through seventeenth-century treaties, including the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658 concluded by Charles X Gustav.

hamadan.s: Hamadan is a city in western Iran, identified with ancient Ecbatana. According to Herodotus, the Median unifier Deioces established Ecbatana as the capital of the Medes.

hamburg.s: Hamburg is a major port city in northern Germany on the River Elbe. As a free imperial city and member of the Hanseatic League, it developed a commercial economy largely independent of imperial direction.

hammurabi.s: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon who reigned c. 1792–1750 BCE and built the Babylonian Empire across Mesopotamia.

han-campaigns-against-the-xiongnu-120s-1.n: Han campaigns against the Xiongnu (120s–110s BCE)
han-campaigns-against-the-xiongnu-120s-1.s: The Han campaigns against the Xiongnu of the 120s and 110s BCE were a series of large offensives launched by the Han Dynasty under Emperor Wu into the steppe. Commanders such as Wei Qing and Huo Qubing drove deep into Xiongnu territory and seized key pasture lands.

han-chinese.s: The Han Chinese are the majority ethnic group of China, taking their name from the Han Dynasty. They were the core population of native dynasties such as the Ming Empire.

han-dynasty.s: The Han Dynasty ruled China from 202 BCE to 220 CE, with a brief interruption, and is regarded as a formative era of Chinese civilisation. It consolidated centralised bureaucratic government, Confucian state ideology and the Silk Road trade.

han-river.s: The Han River is a major tributary of the Yangtze in central China. The twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng on its banks guarded the approach to the Yangtze valley.

han-system.s: The han system was the organisation of Tokugawa Japan into domains, called han, each governed by a daimyo who owed allegiance to the shogun. The domains kept considerable autonomy in local administration while the shogunate controlled national affairs.

hanafi-school.s: The Hanafi school is one of the four main schools of Sunni Islamic law, named after the eighth-century jurist Abu Hanifa. It is known for its use of reasoning and was widely followed in Central Asia and the Turkic world.

hand-cannon.s: The hand cannon was an early firearm consisting of a simple metal tube fired by igniting gunpowder by hand. It developed in China and spread widely in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

handover-of-hong-kong.s: The Handover of Hong Kong was the transfer of sovereignty over Hong Kong from the United Kingdom to the People's Republic of China in 1997. It ended more than a century and a half of British rule over the territory.

hanging-gardens-of-babylon.s: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were a legendary terraced garden listed among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Tradition attributes them to Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire, though no definite archaeological trace has been found and their location remains debated.

hangzhou.s: Hangzhou, known in the Song period as Lin'an, is a city in eastern China at the southern end of the Grand Canal. It became the capital of the Southern Song after the loss of northern China to the Jin.

hanigalbat.s: Hanigalbat was the name used for the reduced Mitanni state after its defeat by the Hittites. After Suppiluliuma I sacked Washukanni around 1340 BCE, Mitanni's territory was confined largely to the Khabur valley.

hannibal.s: Hannibal Barca was a Carthaginian general who led the invasion of Italy during the Second Punic War. After crossing the Alps he won major victories over Rome, including at Cannae, but could not force Rome to surrender.

hannibals-crossing-of-the-alps.s: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps was the march of a Carthaginian army, including war elephants, from Iberia over the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE. It opened the Second Punic War with an invasion of the Roman heartland.

hanno-the-navigator.s: Hanno the Navigator was a Carthaginian explorer who led a voyage along the Atlantic coast of West Africa around 500 BCE. An account of the voyage survives in a Greek version known as a periplus, and how far he reached remains debated.

hanoi.s: Hanoi is a city in northern Vietnam on the Red River, the historic centre of Vietnamese states. Under the French Empire it became the seat of the governor-general of French Indochina.

hanren.s: Hanren was the term used under the Yuan Dynasty for the inhabitants of northern China, including Han Chinese and others who had lived under the Jin. They formed the third tier of the Yuan four-class hierarchy, below the Mongols and Semu but above the southern Chinese, or Nanren.

hanseatic-league.s: The Hanseatic League was a commercial and defensive association of merchant guilds and towns in northern Europe, active from the medieval period into the early modern era. Led by cities such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Bremen, it dominated trade in the Baltic and North Sea.

han-xiongnu-war.s: The Han–Xiongnu War was a long series of conflicts between the Han Dynasty and the Xiongnu confederation, entering its offensive phase from 129 BCE under Emperor Wu. Han armies campaigned deep into the steppe and secured the Hexi Corridor.

harar.s: Harar is a walled city in eastern Ethiopia, a centre of Islamic learning and trade. It became the capital of the Adal Sultanate and the base for campaigns against the Christian Ethiopian state.

harari.s: The Harari are a Semitic-speaking Muslim people of the city of Harar in eastern Ethiopia. They were closely associated with the Adal Sultanate.

harem-conspiracy.s: The Harem conspiracy was a plot within the royal household against Pharaoh Ramesses III of Egypt around 1153 BCE. Records of the trial of the conspirators survive, and forensic study of his mummy indicates that he was killed.

harold-macmillan.s: Harold Macmillan was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1957 to 1963. In his 1960 'Wind of Change' speech in South Africa he acknowledged the strength of African nationalism.

harran.s: Harran is an ancient city in upper Mesopotamia, in present-day south-eastern Turkey, known as a centre of the moon god Sin. After the fall of Nineveh, the last Assyrian king Ashur-uballit II made a final stand there.

harris-papyrus.s: The Harris Papyrus is a long Egyptian papyrus from the reign of Ramesses III's successor, recording the king's donations to temples. It shows that the temples of Amun owned vast lands and resources.

harris-treaty.s: The Harris Treaty of 1858, formally the Treaty of Amity and Commerce, was concluded between the United States and Japan through the American consul Townsend Harris. It opened ports to trade and granted extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs.

harry-rawson.s: Harry Rawson was a British admiral who commanded the Punitive Expedition against Benin in 1897. The expedition followed the killing of a British delegation and resulted in the burning of Benin City, the looting of the palace and the exile of Oba Ovonramwen.

harun-al-rashid.s: Harun al-Rashid was Abbasid caliph who reigned from 786 to 809. His reign is remembered as a high point of Abbasid prosperity and culture in Baghdad and is immortalised in The Thousand and One Nights.

hasan-ibn-ali.s: Hasan ibn Ali was a grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the elder son of Ali, the fourth Rashidun caliph. After Ali's assassination in 661 he was briefly recognised as caliph in Kufa.

hasan-i-sabbah.s: Hasan-i Sabbah was an Ismaili missionary who founded the Nizari branch after the succession crisis of 1094 in the Fatimid Caliphate. From the fortress of Alamut in the Alborz Mountains of Iran he built a network of strongholds.

hasidism.s: Hasidism is a Jewish religious movement founded in the eighteenth century in Eastern Europe, emphasising mysticism, joyful worship and devotion to charismatic leaders. It arose among the Jewish communities of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

hasmonean-dynasty.s: The Hasmonean dynasty ruled Judea in the second and first centuries BCE. It arose from the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid Empire, sparked by religious persecution and Hellenising pressures.

hassan-tower.s: The Hassan Tower is the unfinished minaret of a great mosque in Rabat, Morocco, begun under the Almohad caliph Yaqub al-Mansur in the late twelfth century. The mosque was never completed.

hatshepsut.s: Hatshepsut was a female pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt who ruled c. 1479–1458 BCE.

hatti.s: Hatti was the ancient name for the land of central Anatolia that formed the core of the Hittite kingdom. In the Bronze Age it was a major power competing with Mitanni and Egypt.

hattians.s: The Hattians were the earlier inhabitants of central Anatolia, speaking a non-Indo-European language, before the rise of the Hittites. The Hittites adopted the land's name, Hatti, and absorbed many Hattian religious traditions and deities.

hattusa.s: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, located near present-day Boğazkale in central Turkey. The site has yielded large archives of cuneiform tablets, monumental gates and temples.

hattusili-i.s: Hattusili I was an early king of the Hittites, regarded as one of the founders of the Hittite kingdom. He is associated with making Hattusa the capital and with campaigns into northern Syria.

hattusili-iii.s: Hattusili III was a king of the Hittite Empire in the thirteenth century BCE. He concluded a peace treaty with Ramesses II of Egypt, one of the earliest known international peace treaties.

hausa.s: The Hausa are a people of northern Nigeria and southern Niger, whose city-states such as Kano and Katsina were important centres of trade and crafts. The Kanem-Bornu Empire interacted with and at times exercised influence over them.

hayam-wuruk.s: Hayam Wuruk was king of Majapahit who reigned from 1350 to 1389 CE. With his chief minister Gajah Mada he presided over the height of Majapahit power, when its influence extended across much of the Indonesian archipelago.

hayreddin-barbarossa.s: Hayreddin Barbarossa was a sixteenth-century corsair who became grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet. He secured Algiers for the Ottomans and won a major victory over a Christian fleet at Preveza in 1538.

hazara.s: Hazara is a region in present-day north-western Pakistan. An uprising there, alongside that at Multan, helped trigger the Second Anglo-Sikh War of 1848–1849.

heavenly-khagan.s: Heavenly Khagan was the title granted by steppe peoples to Emperor Taizong of the Tang Dynasty. It recognised him as overlord of the Turkic world as well as emperor of China.

heavy-cavalry.s: Heavy cavalry refers to mounted troops with substantial armour and weapons, used for shock action against enemy formations. The Sasanian Empire fielded armoured cavalry as the core of its army, which the Rashidun Caliphate faced in its conquests.

heavy-taxation.s: Heavy taxation is a recurring pattern in which rulers raise tax burdens to fund wars, armies or courts, provoking rural distress, revolt and loss of legitimacy. Excessive demands can erode the economic base on which the state depends.

hebei.s: Hebei is a province of northern China surrounding present-day Beijing. Under the Song Dynasty it was an important region for coal and iron production on a large scale.

hebrew.s: Hebrew is a Semitic language, the language of the Hebrew Bible and of ancient Israel. Hebrew scripture records the impact of Assyrian, Babylonian and Chaldean power on the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

hebrew-bible.s: The Hebrew Bible is the collection of scriptures of Judaism, also forming the Old Testament of Christianity. It records the conquests of the Assyrian Empire and the Babylonian exile.

heeren-xvii.s: The Heeren XVII, or Seventeen Lords, was the governing board of the Dutch East India Company, composed of delegates from its regional chambers. It set policy for the company's trade, fleets and overseas posts.

heinrich-barth.s: Heinrich Barth was a German explorer and scholar who travelled extensively in North and West Africa in the mid-nineteenth century. His detailed accounts of the Sokoto Caliphate and neighbouring states documented their trade, society and history.

hejaz.s: The Hejaz is a region of western Arabia along the Red Sea, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. Control or protection of the Hejaz brought great prestige to Muslim rulers, including the Ayyubid Empire and the Mamluk Sultanate.

hellenistic-period.s: The Hellenistic period is the era from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE to the late first century BCE, when Greek culture spread across the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia. It was dominated by the successor kingdoms, including the Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires.

hellenization.s: Hellenisation refers to the spread of Greek language, culture, institutions and urban life among non-Greek peoples, especially after the conquests of Alexander the Great. It was promoted through new cities, gymnasia and Greek administration.

hellespont.s: The Hellespont, now known as the Dardanelles, is the narrow strait linking the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara and separating Europe from Asia. Xerxes famously bridged it to invade Greece.

helmuth-von-moltke-the-elder.s: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder was a Prussian field marshal and long-serving chief of the Prussian General Staff. He directed the victories over Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–1871, using railways and staff planning to great effect.

henri-matisse.s: Henri Matisse was a French painter, one of the leading figures of modern art in the twentieth century. Along with Picasso and others, he admired African art that reached European collections.

henrician-articles.s: The Henrician Articles were a set of constitutional principles adopted in 1573 and sworn by each newly elected king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, named after the first elected king, Henry of Valois. They guaranteed free royal election, regular sessions of the Sejm,…

henry-wadsworth-longfellow.s: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was a nineteenth-century American poet, author of works such as The Song of Hiawatha. Emperor Pedro II of the Brazilian Empire corresponded with him.

hephthalites.s: The Hephthalites were a people of Central Asia who built a powerful state in Bactria and neighbouring regions in the fifth and sixth centuries CE. They threatened the Sasanian Empire's north-eastern frontier.

heqin.s: Heqin, meaning 'harmonious kinship', was a Chinese policy of making peace with steppe powers through marriage alliances and regular gifts of silk, grain and other goods. The Han Dynasty adopted it towards the Xiongnu after early military setbacks.

heraclius.s: Heraclius was a Byzantine emperor of the early seventh century who fought a long war against the Sasanian Empire. After major Persian advances, he campaigned deep into Persian territory and won a decisive victory in 627, forcing peace.

herat.s: Herat is a city in western Afghanistan, historically a major centre of Khorasan. Under the Timurid Empire, especially in the fifteenth century, it became a capital and a leading centre of Persian art, literature and scholarship.

herat-school.s: The Herat school was a tradition of Persian miniature painting and book arts that flourished in Herat under Timurid patronage, especially in the late fifteenth century. Its most celebrated master was Bihzad.

hernan-cortes.s: Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led the expedition that brought down the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521. Allied with indigenous peoples such as the Tlaxcalans, he captured the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan.

herodotus.s: Herodotus was a Greek historian of the fifth century BCE, often called the father of history, whose Histories describe the peoples of the Persian world and the Greco-Persian Wars. He is a key source for the Median Empire, crediting Deioces with its unification.

hetman.s: Hetman was the title of the highest military commander in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, with separate grand and field hetmans for the Crown and Lithuania. Hetmans held their posts for life and enjoyed considerable independence from the king.

high-priest-of-amun.s: The High Priest of Amun was the chief priest of the god Amun at Thebes, controlling the god's vast temple estates. As royal power weakened in the late Twentieth Dynasty, the high priests became a rival authority to the pharaoh.

hijra.s: The Hijra was the migration of the Prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar. In Medina the first Muslim community-state was formed, the basis of the later Rashidun Caliphate.

hijra-of-usman-dan-fodio.s: The Hijra of Usman dan Fodio was the migration of the reformer and his followers to Gudu in 1804, modelled on the Prophet Muhammad's hijra. There his community elected him Commander of the Faithful, and he declared jihad against the Hausa kings.

hill-fort.s: A hill fort is a fortification built on high ground, using the natural terrain for defence. In the Deccan, Shivaji and his successors made extensive use of hill forts as anchors of Maratha resistance, combined with guerrilla tactics.

himilco.s: Himilco was a Carthaginian navigator who sailed northward along the Atlantic coast of Europe. His voyage is associated with access to tin-producing regions of north-western Europe.

himyarite-kingdom.s: The Himyarite Kingdom was a state in southern Arabia, in present-day Yemen, that dominated the region in late antiquity. Its rulers adopted Judaism in the late period.

hindu-kush.s: The Hindu Kush is a mountain range in Afghanistan and northern Pakistan that separates Central Asia from the Indian subcontinent. Its passes were the routes used by invaders entering India from the north-west.

hindu-revivalism.s: Hindu revivalism refers to movements asserting Hindu political and cultural identity, particularly in response to Muslim rule in India. Shivaji's coronation in 1674 drew on such ideas, establishing a monarchy rooted in Marathi culture and Hindu tradition.

hindu-buddhist.s: Hindu-Buddhist refers to the blended religious and cultural tradition, drawing on both Hinduism and Buddhism, that shaped many states of South-East Asia. The Majapahit Empire was its last great expression in the Indonesian archipelago.

hinduism.s: Hinduism is a major religious tradition of South Asia, encompassing diverse beliefs, practices and scriptures. It shaped kingship and temple building in the Khmer Empire and was central to the identity of the Maratha Empire.

hindustan.s: Hindustan is a historical name for northern India, particularly the plains of the Indus and Ganges. In 1229 the Abbasid caliph recognised Iltutmish as Sultan of Hindustan, giving the Delhi Sultanate international Islamic legitimacy.

hirohito.s: Hirohito was Emperor of Japan from 1926 until his death in 1989. His reign saw Japanese militarism, expansion in Asia and the Pacific War.

hiroshima.s: Hiroshima is a city in western Japan. On 6 August 1945 it became the first city to be destroyed by an atomic bomb, dropped by the United States.

hittite-empire.s: The Hittite Empire was a major Bronze Age state centred on Hattusa in central Anatolia, at its height in the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BCE. It rivalled Egypt and destroyed the power of Mitanni, and earlier sacked Babylon.

hittite-laws.s: The Hittite laws are a collection of legal provisions from the Hittite kingdom, preserved on cuneiform tablets from Hattusa. They cover matters such as property, family, agriculture and crime, often favouring compensation over harsh physical punishment.

hittite-sack-of-babylon.s: The Hittite sack of Babylon was a raid on Babylon led by the Hittite king Mursili I around c. 1595 BCE.

hittite-sack-of-washukanni.s: The Hittite sack of Washukanni was the capture of the Mitanni capital by the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I around c. 1340 BCE.

hittite-vassal-treaties.s: The Hittite vassal treaties were formal agreements between Hittite kings and subordinate rulers, recorded on cuneiform tablets. They typically set out the history of relations, obligations of loyalty and tribute, and divine witnesses and curses.

hoechst.s: Hoechst was a German chemical and pharmaceutical company founded in the nineteenth century. Together with BASF and Bayer, it led the German chemical industry, which dominated world synthetic dye production before the First World War.

holkars.s: The Holkars were a Maratha ruling family who governed Indore in central India. They were one of the major chiefly houses, alongside the Scindias, Gaekwads and Bhonsles, that held power in the Maratha confederacy.

holy-roman-emperor.s: The Holy Roman Emperor was the elected ruler of the Holy Roman Empire, a title that originated with Otto I's coronation in 962 CE and was formally given up by Francis II in 1806. Charles V held it alongside the Spanish crown.

holy-roman-empire.s: The Holy Roman Empire was a complex political union of territories in central Europe that existed from 962 to 1806. It claimed succession to the Roman and Carolingian imperial traditions, with an elected emperor presiding over many semi-independent princes and cities.

holy-synod.s: The Holy Synod was the governing body of the Russian Orthodox Church established by Peter the Great in 1721, replacing the office of patriarch. It was overseen by a lay official appointed by the tsar.

hong-kong.s: Hong Kong is a territory on the southern coast of China. It was ceded to Britain after the First Opium War, a symbol of the Qing Empire's humiliation by Western powers.

hong-taiji.s: Hong Taiji was the son and successor of Nurhaci as leader of the Manchus. He renamed his people Manchu and proclaimed the Qing dynasty in 1636, while extending Manchu power over Mongolia and Korea.

hongwu-emperor.s: The Hongwu Emperor, born Zhu Yuanzhang, was a peasant-born rebel leader who founded the Ming dynasty in 1368. He drove the Mongol Yuan court out of China, ending the Yuan Dynasty.

honorius.s: Honorius was Roman emperor in the West from 395 CE, the son of Theodosius I. On his father's death the empire was divided between Honorius in the West and his brother Arcadius in the East, and it was never reunited.

hoplite.s: A hoplite was a heavily armed Greek infantryman, equipped with a large round shield, spear and armour, fighting in the close formation known as the phalanx. Hoplite armies proved effective against the lighter-armed Persian infantry.

hormuz.s: Hormuz is an island and historic trading port at the entrance to the Persian Gulf. It was held by the Portuguese from the early sixteenth century.

horn-of-africa.s: The Horn of Africa is the peninsula of north-eastern Africa comprising present-day Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia. It was the arena of rivalry between the Adal Sultanate and the Ethiopian Empire.

horse-archer.s: A horse archer is a mounted warrior who shoots with a bow from horseback, combining mobility with missile firepower. Horse archers were the hallmark of steppe and Iranian armies.

horse-breeding.s: Horse breeding is the raising of horses for transport, warfare and trade. It underpinned the military power of many empires.

horse-trade.s: The horse trade refers to the exchange of horses, often over long distances, for military and prestige purposes. In the central Sudan, horses imported from North Africa across the Sahara were vital to cavalry warfare.

house-of-aviz.s: The House of Aviz was the royal dynasty of Portugal from 1385 to 1580, founded by King John I. Under its rule, notably with the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator, Portugal began its overseas expansion along the African coast.

house-of-bourbon.s: The House of Bourbon was a European royal dynasty that ruled France and, from the early eighteenth century, Spain. The Spanish Bourbons introduced administrative and fiscal reforms in the empire.

house-of-wettin.s: The House of Wettin was a German dynasty that ruled Saxony. Two of its members, Augustus II and Augustus III, were elected kings of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the eighteenth century.

house-of-wisdom.s: The House of Wisdom, or Bayt al-Hikma, was a major intellectual institution in Baghdad under the Abbasid Caliphate. It is associated with the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and with advances in mathematics, astronomy and other sciences.

hoysala-empire.s: The Hoysala Empire was a kingdom in southern India, centred on present-day Karnataka, known for its ornate temple architecture. Its capital was Dwarasamudra.

huai-army.s: The Huai Army was a regional army raised by Li Hongzhang in the mid-nineteenth century to fight the Taiping and other rebellions. Like the Xiang Army of Zeng Guofan, it succeeded where the Qing regular forces failed.

huang-chao-rebellion.s: The Huang Chao Rebellion was a large uprising in China from 874 to 884, led by the salt smuggler Huang Chao. The rebels ravaged much of the country and captured both Guangzhou and the capital Chang'an.

huang-lao-taoism.s: Huang-Lao Taoism was a school of thought combining Taoist ideas with practical statecraft, named after the Yellow Emperor and Laozi. It favoured minimal government interference and light taxation.

hudson-bay.s: Hudson Bay is a large inland sea in north-eastern Canada. It became the domain of the English Hudson's Bay Company's fur trade from the late seventeenth century.

huerta.s: A huerta is an irrigated agricultural area in Spain, especially around Valencia, Murcia and Granada, using irrigation channels developed in the Islamic period. These areas produced rich crops of fruit, vegetables and other produce.

huexotzinca.s: The Huexotzinca were the people of Huexotzinco, an independent city-state in central Mexico. Along with Tlaxcala, it was a regular opponent of the Aztec Empire in the Flower Wars.

huey-tlatoani.s: Huey Tlatoani, meaning Great Speaker, was the title of the supreme ruler of Tenochtitlan and the Aztec Triple Alliance. The holder was chosen from the royal lineage by a council of nobles.

hugo-grotius.s: Hugo Grotius was a seventeenth-century Dutch jurist, a founder of modern international law. His works addressed the law of war and peace and freedom of the seas.

huhanye.s: Huhanye was a chanyu, or supreme ruler, of the Southern Xiongnu during the succession conflicts of the mid-first century BCE. In 51 BCE he submitted to Han suzerainty, travelling in person to the Han court in exchange for protection and trade privileges.

huitzilopochtli.s: Huitzilopochtli was the Aztec god of the sun and war and the patron deity of the Mexica. According to tradition, he guided the Mexica on their migration to the site of Tenochtitlan.

huizi.s: Huizi was a form of paper money issued by the Southern Song government from the twelfth century. It circulated widely as the state turned to paper currency to meet its fiscal needs.

hulagu-khan.s: Hulagu Khan was a Mongol prince, a grandson of Genghis Khan, who led the Mongol campaigns into south-western Asia in the 1250s. In 1258 his forces sacked Baghdad and executed the caliph, ending the Abbasid Caliphate.

human-sacrifice.s: Human sacrifice is the ritual killing of people as an offering to gods or spirits. In the Aztec Empire it was central to religion, intended to sustain the gods and the cosmic order.

humban-haltash-iii.s: Humban-haltash III was the last known king of Elam. After Ashurbanipal of Assyria destroyed Susa in 646 BCE, he was captured in 640 BCE and paraded as a prisoner.

humban-nikash-i.s: Humban-nikash I was a king of Elam in the Neo-Elamite period. He defeated the Assyrian king Sargon II at the Battle of Der in 721 BCE.

humphrey-gilbert.s: Sir Humphrey Gilbert was an English soldier and explorer of the Elizabethan era. In 1583 he made a formal claim to Newfoundland for the English crown, but was lost at sea on the return voyage and left no settlers.

huna-people.s: The Huna were Central Asian invaders, related to the Hephthalites, who pressed into north-western India from the mid-fifth century CE. Under leaders such as Toramana and Mihirakula they occupied large parts of north-western India.

hundred-days-reform.s: The Hundred Days' Reform was a programme of modernising reforms launched by the Guangxu Emperor in 1898, covering education, administration and the economy. It was ended after about a hundred days by a conservative coup backed by the Empress Dowager Cixi.

hungarian-diet.s: The Hungarian Diet was the parliament of the Kingdom of Hungary. After the Compromise of 1867 it governed Hungary's internal affairs within the Dual Monarchy, while sharing foreign policy, defence and related finance with Austria.

hungarian-revolution-of-1848.s: The Hungarian Revolution of 1848 was an uprising seeking Hungarian autonomy and then independence from Habsburg rule, part of the wider revolutions of 1848 in Europe. It was crushed in 1849 with the help of Russian troops sent by Tsar Nicholas I.

hungary.s: Hungary is a country in central Europe on the Carpathian Basin. Much of it was conquered by the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century and later recovered by the Habsburgs.

huns.s: The Huns were a nomadic people who appeared on the edges of Europe in the late fourth century CE and built a powerful empire, most famously under Attila. Some historians have proposed that they were linked to the Xiongnu, though the connection remains debated.

huo-qubing.s: Huo Qubing was a Han Dynasty general of the second century BCE, renowned for his cavalry campaigns against the Xiongnu under Emperor Wu. His deep raids into the steppe inflicted major defeats and helped secure the Hexi Corridor.

huopao.s: Huopao were incendiary bombs or fire projectiles used in Chinese warfare, often launched by trebuchets. The Song Dynasty developed a range of gunpowder weapons, including such bombs.

hurrians.s: The Hurrians were a people of the ancient Near East, speaking a language unrelated to Semitic or Indo-European tongues, who were widespread in northern Mesopotamia, Syria and Anatolia. They formed the main population of the Mitanni Empire, ruled by an Indo-Aryan elite.

husayn-bayqara.s: Husayn Bayqara was a Timurid ruler of Herat who reigned from 1469 to 1506. His court was a brilliant centre of Persian and Chagatai literature, painting and architecture, with figures such as the poet Ali-Shir Nava'i and the painter Bihzad.

husayn-ibn-ali.s: Husayn ibn Ali was a grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the son of Ali, the fourth caliph. He refused to recognise the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and was killed with his companions at Karbala in 680 CE.

hyksos.s: The Hyksos were a people of West Asian origin who ruled northern Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period. They introduced or popularised technologies such as the horse-drawn chariot and composite bow.

hypaspists.s: The hypaspists were an elite infantry corps in the Macedonian army of Philip II and Alexander the Great. They fought alongside the phalanx and were used for demanding tasks.

henry-ii-of-england.s: Henry II of England, the first Plantagenet king, ruled England, Normandy, Anjou and, through his wife Eleanor, Aquitaine, a block of lands known as the Angevin Empire. He reformed English law and royal justice.

henry-ii-of-france.s: Henry II of France, son of Francis I, was king of France from 1547 to 1559. As dauphin he was the last separate Duke of Brittany, so his accession merged the duchy's title with the crown.

henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor, was the last Ottonian ruler, king of Germany from 1002 and emperor from 1014. He defeated the Italian rival king Arduin of Ivrea and fought long wars with Bolesław I of Poland, ended by the Peace of Bautzen in 1018.

henry-ii-the-pious.s: Henry II the Pious was Duke of Silesia and high duke of Poland from 1238, son of Henry the Bearded and Saint Hedwig. Like his father he sought to reunite the divided Polish duchies.

henry-ii-duke-of-guise.s: Henry II, Duke of Guise, was a French noble of the house of Lorraine who claimed the Angevin inheritance to the throne of Naples. Invited by the rebels of the Neapolitan Republic, he arrived in Naples in late 1647 and took the title of duke of the republic.

henry-the-lion.s: Henry the Lion was a Welf prince, Duke of Saxony from 1142 and Duke of Bavaria from 1156, the most powerful German noble of his age. He conquered Slavic lands east of the Elbe, refounded Lübeck and Munich, and set up bishoprics in Ratzeburg and Schwerin.

harald-fairhair.s: Harald Fairhair is remembered as the first king of a united Norway. According to the sagas he subdued the petty kingdoms of the west coast and won the Battle of Hafrsfjord, traditionally dated around 872.

hyder-ali.s: Hyder Ali was a soldier who rose to command the army of the Kingdom of Mysore and from 1761 ruled it in place of the Wodeyar kings. He conquered Keladi, Chitradurga and Malabar, invaded Coorg, and built a modern army with French help.

henry-the-fowler.s: Henry the Fowler, Duke of Saxony, was elected king of East Francia in 919, the first of the Ottonian dynasty. He won over the dukes of Swabia and Bavaria, regained Lotharingia, campaigned against the Slavs east of the Elbe, taking Brandenburg from the Hevelli, and defeated the…

harry-johnston.s: Sir Harry Johnston was a British explorer and colonial administrator. As vice-consul in the Niger Delta he deported King Jaja of Opobo in 1887.

henry-iv-of-france.s: Henry IV of France was king of Navarre from 1572 and the first Bourbon king of France from 1589. A Protestant leader in the Wars of Religion, he converted to Catholicism in 1593 to win Paris and issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, granting toleration to Huguenots.

henry-iv-of-england.s: Henry IV of England, Henry Bolingbroke, deposed his cousin Richard II in 1399 and founded the Lancastrian dynasty. His reign was spent putting down rebellions by the Percys and by Owain Glyndŵr in Wales.

henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor.s: Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor, was king of Germany from 1056 and emperor from 1084. His clash with Pope Gregory VII over the appointment of bishops began the Investiture Controversy, and he did penance at Canossa in 1077.

hudsons-bay-company.s: The Hudson's Bay Company was chartered by Charles II in 1670 with a monopoly of trade in all lands draining into Hudson Bay, a territory called Rupert's Land. It ran the fur trade with Cree, Assiniboine and other peoples from posts on the bay and later across the west, merging…

halfdan-the-black.s: Halfdan the Black was a king of Vestfold in south-eastern Norway, known only from later sagas, above all Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla. The son of Gudrød the Hunter and Åsa of Agder, he is said to have extended his rule over Hadeland, Raumarike, Hedmark and other inland…

henri-gouraud.s: Henri Gouraud was a French general who served in West Africa, capturing Samori Ture in 1898 and conquering the Adrar of Mauritania in 1909, and later commanded at Gallipoli and on the Western Front. As French High Commissioner in the Levant from 1919 to 1923 he defeated…

hugh-capet.s: Hugh Capet was Duke of the Franks and, from 987, King of the Franks, the founder of the Capetian dynasty. Son of Hugh the Great, he held lands around Paris and Orléans and was elected king at Senlis after the death of the last Carolingian king, Louis V.

hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath.n: Hugh de Lacy, Lord of Meath
hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath.s: Hugh de Lacy was an Anglo-Norman baron who in 1172 received from Henry II the former Kingdom of Mide as the Lordship of Meath, to balance Strongbow's power in Leinster. He built motte castles and Trim Castle, settled English tenants and served as the king's governor in Ireland.

hugh-de-lacy-earl-of-ulster.n: Hugh de Lacy, Earl of Ulster
hugh-de-lacy-earl-of-ulster.s: Hugh de Lacy, a younger son of the Lord of Meath, was made Earl of Ulster by King John in 1205 after he had driven out John de Courcy. He lost his lands when John campaigned in Ireland in 1210, fled to France and fought in the Albigensian Crusade, returning to recover the…

hun-sen.s: Hun Sen is a Cambodian politician, a former Khmer Rouge commander who fled to Vietnam in 1977 and returned with the Vietnamese invasion of 1979. He became foreign minister and in 1985 prime minister of the People's Republic of Kampuchea, continued in the State of Cambodia, and…

han-guang.s: Han Guang was a commander sent north by Wu Chen, the rebel king of Zhao, during the revolt against the Qin, who instead made himself King of Yan in 209 BCE. When Xiang Yu divided China into the Eighteen Kingdoms in 206 BCE, he moved Han Guang to the remote Kingdom of Liaodong…

han-xin.s: Han Xin was the leading general of Liu Bang in the Chu–Han war that founded the Han dynasty. Having deserted Xiang Yu, he took the Qin heartland in 206 BCE, captured Wei Bao in 205 BCE by crossing the Yellow River on rafts, conquered Zhao and Qi, and made himself King of Qi in…

huang-chao.s: Huang Chao was a failed examination candidate and salt smuggler who led the largest rebellion of the late Tang dynasty. Rising in 875, his army marched through much of China, sacked Guangzhou in 879 and took Chang'an in 881, where he proclaimed the state of Qi.

hugh-of-arles.s: Hugh of Arles, also called Hugh of Provence, was count of Arles and Vienne and effective ruler of Provence before becoming King of Italy in 926. He sought to control Rome through marriage to Marozia but was driven out by her son Alberic II in 932.

hugh-the-great.s: Hugh the Great was a Robertian count of Paris and Duke of the Franks, the most powerful noble of West Francia in the 10th century. Son of King Robert I, he did not take the crown himself, but in 936 brought the Carolingian Louis IV back from England and was recognised as duke…

hugh-of-tuscany.s: Hugh, also called Hugh the Great, was Margrave of Tuscany from the 960s and for a time Duke of Spoleto and Camerino, a loyal supporter of the Ottonian emperors in Italy. He ruled from Lucca and Florence and endowed monasteries, among them the Badia of Florence founded by his…

hadrians-wall.s: Hadrian's Wall is a Roman frontier wall across northern England from the Tyne to the Solway Firth, begun in 122 CE on the orders of Emperor Hadrian. With forts, milecastles and a ditch, it marked the northern frontier of Roman Britain for most of three centuries.

henry-of-livonia.s: Henry of Livonia was a priest who took part in the German crusades in the eastern Baltic and wrote the Livonian Chronicle, covering events to 1227. It is the main source for the conquest and conversion of the Livs, Latvians and Estonians.

ho-quy-ly.s: Hồ Quý Ly was a powerful minister of the Trần dynasty who deposed the last Trần emperor in 1400 and founded the Hồ dynasty. He carried out radical reforms, issuing paper money, limiting landholdings and building a stone citadel at Tây Đô.

hoa-lu.s: Hoa Lư was the capital of Vietnam from 968 to 1010, in present-day Ninh Bình province. Đinh Tiên Hoàng built it as a fortified capital among limestone hills, and the Early Lê kept it. In 1010 Lý Thái Tổ moved the capital to Thăng Long, modern Hanoi; temples to the Đinh and Lê…

huai-river.s: The Huai River flows east across central China between the Yellow River and the Yangtze, and is often treated as the line between northern and southern China. Its plain was home to many small Zhou-era states, later absorbed by Chu.

huan-xuan.s: Huan Xuan was a warlord of the Eastern Jin dynasty and son of the powerful general Huan Wen. From his base in the middle Yangtze he took the capital Jiankang in 402 and in 403 forced Emperor An to abdicate, proclaiming his own dynasty of Chu.

huayna-capac.s: Huayna Capac was the Sapa Inca who ruled the Inca Empire at its greatest extent, from about 1493. He campaigned in the north, crushing the Caranqui and Cayambi and making Quito a northern capital.

hywel-dda.s: Hywel Dda, Hywel the Good, was a Welsh king, grandson of Rhodri the Great. He inherited Seisyllwg, united it with Dyfed around 920 to form Deheubarth and later ruled most of Wales.

henry-of-flanders.s: Henry of Flanders was Latin Emperor of Constantinople from 1205, succeeding his brother Baldwin I. He was the ablest of the Latin emperors, defending the empire against the Bulgarians and the Nicaeans and conciliating the Greeks.

henry-v-holy-roman-emperor.s: Henry V was the last Salian King of Germany, from 1106, and Holy Roman Emperor from 1111. He continued the Investiture Controversy with the papacy until the Concordat of Worms in 1122.

hamir-singh-of-faridkot.s: Hamir Singh was a Brar Jat Sikh chief who established himself at Faridkot around 1763, as Sikh power spread across the Malwa plains of Punjab after the Durrani wars, founding the ruling house of Faridkot State. His descendants ruled as Rajas, under British protection from the…

hamir-singh-of-nabha.s: Hamir Singh was a Phulkian Sikh chief, descended from Phul and a kinsman of the rulers of Patiala, who founded the state of Nabha in the Malwa region of Punjab in the 1750s. He took part in the Sikh capture of Sirhind in 1764 and struck his own coins.

hassan-gouled-aptidon.s: Hassan Gouled Aptidon was an Issa Somali politician who represented French Somaliland in the French parliament and later led the campaign for independence. He became the first president of Djibouti at independence in 1977 and ruled until 1999.

hedayat-allah-khan.s: Hedayat-Allah Khan was ruler of Gilan on the Caspian coast of Iran in the second half of the 18th century, from a notable family of Fuman. He made Rasht his capital and grew rich from the province's silk trade with Russia, while acknowledging the Zand rulers of Iran when he…

heng-samrin.s: Heng Samrin was a Khmer Rouge commander in Cambodia's Eastern Zone who fled to Vietnam in 1978 to escape the purges. After the Vietnamese invasion of January 1979 he became head of state of the People's Republic of Kampuchea and leader of its ruling party, though real…

henri-christophe.s: Henri Christophe was a general of the Haitian Revolution under Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines. After Dessalines was killed in 1806 he rejected the weak presidency offered by the southern elite and set up the State of Haiti in the north, proclaiming himself…

henry-iii-of-england.s: Henry III was king of England from 1216, succeeding his father John as a nine-year-old. He took the earldom of Chester into royal hands in 1237 and, in the Treaty of Montgomery of 1267, recognised Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales.

henry-iii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Henry III, of the Salian dynasty, was king of Germany from 1039 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1046. At the Synod of Sutri in 1046 he deposed rival popes and went on to install reforming German popes.

henry-iii-of-glogow.s: Henry III was a Silesian Piast duke of Głogów from 1274 and one of the most powerful princes of fragmented Poland. After the death of Wenceslaus III in 1306 he took most of Greater Poland and styled himself heir of the Kingdom of Poland.

henry-vii-of-england.s: Henry VII, born Henry Tudor at Pembroke Castle in 1457, was the Lancastrian claimant who defeated Richard III at Bosworth in 1485 and became king of England, founding the Tudor dynasty. His marriage to Elizabeth of York joined the rival houses of the Wars of the Roses.

henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Henry VII was count of Luxembourg, elected king of Germany in 1308 and crowned emperor in Rome in 1312, the first since Frederick II. On his Italian expedition of 1310–1313 he tried to restore imperial authority, naming imperial vicars such as the Pico at Mirandola and…

herman-willem-daendels.s: Herman Willem Daendels was a Dutch Patriot and general who served as governor-general of the Dutch East Indies from 1808 to 1811 for Louis Bonaparte's Kingdom of Holland. To defend Java against Britain he reorganised its administration, built the Great Post Road along the…

herod-of-chalcis.s: Herod of Chalcis was a grandson of Herod the Great and brother of Agrippa I. In 41 CE the emperor Claudius made him king of Chalcis in the Beqaa valley, and later gave him authority over the Temple in Jerusalem and the right to appoint its high priests.

heydar-aliyev.s: Heydar Aliyev was a KGB officer who led the Communist Party of the Azerbaijan SSR from 1969 to 1982 and then became a member of the Soviet Politburo. He returned to power in independent Azerbaijan in 1993 and as president agreed the 1994 ceasefire in the First Karabakh War and…

haute-cour-kingdom-of-jerusalem.s: The Haute Cour, or High Court, was the feudal council of the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, made up of the king and his tenants-in-chief, the great barons and prelates. It advised the king, judged disputes between vassals, approved laws and taxes and decided disputed…

high-court-of-australia.s: The High Court of Australia is the highest court of the Commonwealth of Australia, provided for in the federal constitution of 1901 and established in 1903. It interprets the constitution, settles disputes between the Commonwealth and the states and hears final appeals.

hikayat-banjar.s: The Hikayat Banjar is the Malay-language royal chronicle of the Banjar Sultanate of South Kalimantan, surviving in versions from the 17th century onwards. It tells of the founding of Negara Dipa by a merchant from Keling, the move of the royal seat to Negara Daha, and the…

ho-chi-minh.s: Ho Chi Minh was a Vietnamese revolutionary who helped found the French Communist Party and the Indochinese Communist Party, and in 1941 formed the Viet Minh. In the August Revolution of 1945 he proclaimed the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi.

hou-jing.s: Hou Jing was a general of Eastern Wei who defected to the southern Liang dynasty after the death of Gao Huan in 547. In 548 he rebelled, besieged the Liang capital Jiankang and took it in 549, and Emperor Wu of Liang died in his hands.

house-of-assembly-of-barbados.s: The House of Assembly is the elected lower house of the Parliament of Barbados, first convened in 1639 and one of the oldest legislatures in the Americas. For centuries it represented the island's white planters and property owners, while the enslaved majority had no voice.

huan-wen.s: Huan Wen was a general and statesman of the Eastern Jin who dominated the court for two decades. He conquered Cheng Han in Sichuan in 347 and led campaigns into the north, retaking Luoyang in 356, but was defeated by the Former Yan general Murong Chui at Fangtou in 369.

hugh-of-saint-omer.s: Hugh of Saint-Omer, also called Hugh of Fauquembergues, was a knight from Artois who came east with the First Crusade. In 1101, when Tancred left for Antioch, King Baldwin I gave him the Principality of Galilee.

hugh-oneill-earl-of-tyrone.s: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, was the most powerful Gaelic lord of Ulster at the end of the 16th century. Raised partly under English influence, he led the Ulster lords, including Red Hugh O'Donnell and Hugh Maguire, in the Nine Years' War against Elizabeth I and won at the…

hungarian-red-army.s: The Hungarian Red Army was the armed force of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, formed in 1919 from remnants of the old army, workers' battalions and volunteers. In May and June it pushed into Slovakia, where the Slovak Soviet Republic was proclaimed under its protection, and it…

hussein-kamel-of-egypt.s: Hussein Kamel was a son of Khedive Ismail and uncle of Abbas II. When Britain declared a protectorate over Egypt in December 1914, deposing Abbas II and ending Ottoman sovereignty, it made Hussein Kamel ruler with the title of sultan, marking the break with Istanbul.

house-of-la-tour-dauvergne.s: The La Tour d'Auvergne were a French noble family named after La Tour in Auvergne. By marriage they acquired the counties of Auvergne and Boulogne in the late 14th century, and in 1444 the Viscounty of Turenne.

hungarian-round-table-talks.s: The Hungarian Round Table Talks were negotiations held from June to September 1989 between the ruling communist party and the opposition. They agreed on free multi-party elections, a constitutional court and a presidency, amending the constitution so that the Republic of…

henry-of-the-palatinate.s: Henry of the Palatinate, a Wittelsbach prince, was bishop of Utrecht from 1524 to 1529 and later of Worms and Freising. Unable to defend his lands against the Duke of Guelders and rebels in Utrecht, he transferred his temporal power to Emperor Charles V in 1528.

house-of-dadiani.s: The House of Dadiani was the Georgian princely family that ruled Mingrelia in western Georgia. Nominal vassals of the kings of Imereti, they were often stronger than their overlords and dominated neighbours such as Abkhazia and Svaneti.

hungarian-declaration-of-independence.s: The Hungarian Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Hungarian parliament at Debrecen on 14 April 1849, during the revolution against Austria. It dethroned the House of Habsburg-Lorraine and made Lajos Kossuth governor-president.

henry-vi-holy-roman-emperor.s: Henry VI was a Hohenstaufen emperor, son of Frederick Barbarossa, crowned emperor in 1191. Through his wife Constance he won the Kingdom of Sicily in 1194.

ha-tien.s: Hà Tiên is a port on the Gulf of Thailand in southern Vietnam, near the Cambodian border. Originally the Cambodian town of Peam, it was developed in the late 17th century by the Chinese exile Mạc Cửu into a trading port, which he placed under Vietnamese Nguyễn protection…

haakon-iv-of-norway.s: Haakon IV of Norway reigned from 1217 and brought the long Norwegian civil wars to an end, defeating the rebel Skule Bårdsson in 1240. His reign is seen as the height of medieval Norway.

hafiz-rahmat-khan.s: Hafiz Rahmat Khan was a Rohilla Afghan leader who governed Rohilkhand as regent for the sons of Ali Muhammad Khan after 1748, leading a confederacy of Rohilla chiefs from Bareilly. He supported Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

hajji-chelebi.s: Hajji Chelebi was a notable of Shaki in north-western Azerbaijan who in 1743 led a rising against the heavy taxes of Nader Shah's Afsharid Empire and defeated the forces sent against him. He made Shaki an independent khanate, the first of the Caucasian khanates to break from…

hamzat-bek.s: Hamzat Bek was the second imam of the Caucasian Imamate, succeeding Ghazi Muhammad after his death at Gimry in 1832. In 1834 he took the Avar capital Khunzakh and massacred the family of the Avar khans.

han-liner.s: Han Lin'er was the son of the White Lotus leader Han Shantong, who launched the Red Turban revolt against the Yuan dynasty in 1351. In 1355 rebel commanders proclaimed him emperor of a restored Song dynasty, and Zhu Yuanzhang rose under his banner.

hari-chand-of-guler.s: Hari Chand was, by tradition, an heir to the throne of Kangra who around 1405 fell into a well while hunting and was presumed dead. His brother took the Kangra throne, and when Hari Chand was rescued he founded a new state with its capital at Haripur.

hasan-ibn-zayd.s: Hasan ibn Zayd was a descendant of the Prophet's grandson Hasan, invited in 864 by the people of Ruyan and Tabaristan, angered by Tahirid land seizures, to lead them. With Daylamite support he took Amol and founded a Zaydi imamate, the Alavid state of Tabaristan, taking the…

hasan-kuchak.s: Hasan Kuchak, 'Little Hasan', was a grandson of the Ilkhanid commander Chupan. After the death of the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id in 1335 he seized Azerbaijan and set up puppet khans such as Sati Beg and Sulayman Khan to legitimise Chupanid rule.

hashim-al-atassi.s: Hashim al-Atassi was a Syrian nationalist politician from Homs. He was prime minister of the Arab Kingdom of Syria in 1920 and later led the National Bloc, presiding over the Constituent Assembly of 1928 that drafted a constitution under the French mandate.

hassani-arabs.s: The Hassani Arabs, or Banu Hassan, were a branch of the Maqil Bedouin who moved into the western Sahara from the 14th century. Their victory over the Berber Zawaya scholarly tribes in the Char Bouba war of the 1670s established a warrior aristocracy over Mauritania, which…

hendrik-carloff.s: Hendrik Carloff was a merchant and colonial agent of the 17th century who served several companies on the Gold Coast. For the Swedish Africa Company he obtained land from Fante rulers and founded Fort Carolusborg at Cape Coast in 1653.

hendrik-witbooi.s: Hendrik Witbooi was the leader of the Witbooi Nama of Gibeon in southern Namibia and the most persistent opponent of German colonial rule there. After resisting the Germans in the 1890s he signed a protection treaty in 1894, but in 1904 he rose against them.

henry-ii-duke-of-austria.s: Henry II Jasomirgott, of the Babenberg family, was Margrave of Austria from 1141 and also Duke of Bavaria. In 1156 he gave up Bavaria to Henry the Lion, and in return Frederick Barbarossa raised Austria to a duchy by the Privilegium Minus, with special inheritance rights.

henry-morgan.s: Henry Morgan was a Welsh privateer based at Port Royal, Jamaica, who led raids on Spanish America, including Portobelo in 1668 and Maracaibo in 1669. In 1671 he crossed the isthmus and sacked Panama City, which was rebuilt on a new site.

henry-morton-stanley.s: Henry Morton Stanley was a Welsh-American journalist and explorer who found David Livingstone in 1871 and crossed Africa in 1874–1877, following the Lualaba and Congo to the Atlantic with help from Tippu Tip. From 1879 he worked for King Leopold II of the Belgians, gathering…

henry-v-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg.s: Henry V, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, known as Henry the Younger, ruled the Principality of Wolfenbüttel from 1514. A fierce Catholic opponent of the Reformation, he was driven out by the Schmalkaldic League in 1542 but returned.

henry-vi-the-good.s: Henry VI the Good was a Piast duke of Wrocław in Silesia from 1311. Pressed by his relatives, who took much of his inheritance, and caught between Bohemia and Poland, he recognised the overlordship of King John of Bohemia in 1327, with Wrocław to pass to Bohemia on his death.

henry-viii-of-england.s: Henry VIII of England reigned from 1509. His search for a male heir led him to break with the papacy and make himself head of the Church of England, dissolve the monasteries and marry six times, including Anne of Cleves, daughter of the Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, in 1540.

herbert-samuel.s: Herbert Samuel was a British Liberal politician and the first practising Jew in a British cabinet. In July 1920 he became the first High Commissioner for Palestine, replacing the military Occupied Enemy Territory Administration with a civil government.

herkus-monte.s: Herkus Monte was a leader of the Natangians, one of the Old Prussian peoples, who had been educated in Germany. He led the Great Prussian Uprising against the Teutonic Order from 1260 and won a major victory at Pokarwis that year.

hermann-billung.s: Hermann Billung was a Saxon noble whom Otto I entrusted around 936 with command against the Slavs along the lower Elbe, the frontier later called the Billung March. He governed Saxony for Otto during the king's absences and is counted as the first Billung duke of Saxony.

hernando-de-soto.s: Hernando de Soto was a Spanish conquistador who took part in the conquest of Peru and in 1539 led a large expedition into the south-eastern interior of North America. Over four years his army marched through the Mississippian chiefdoms, wintering at the Apalachee capital, and…

herod-antipas.s: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Peraea as tetrarch from 4 BCE to 39 CE. He built Tiberias as his capital, had John the Baptist executed and appears in the Gospel accounts of Jesus's trial.

herod-the-great.s: Herod the Great was an Idumaean named king of Judea by the Roman Senate in 40 BCE, who took Jerusalem from the last Hasmonean king in 37 BCE. A Roman client, he rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem and built Caesarea Maritima and fortresses such as Masada.

hippocrates-of-gela.s: Hippocrates of Gela was tyrant of the Greek city of Gela in Sicily from about 498 BCE. He built the first great territorial power in Greek Sicily, subduing Naxos, Leontini and other cities and defeating Syracuse, from which he took Kamarina and refounded it.

hojo-soun.s: Hōjō Sōun, born Ise Moritoki, was a minor shogunal official with ties to the Imagawa who helped settle their succession dispute in Suruga after 1476. In the 1490s he seized Izu and Odawara castle, becoming one of the first Sengoku warlords.

holy-cross-abbey.s: Holy Cross Abbey is a Cistercian abbey on the River Suir in County Tipperary, refounded around 1180 under the patronage of Domnall Mór O'Brien, king of Thomond. It held a relic of the True Cross and became a major place of pilgrimage.

hong-xiuquan.s: Hong Xiuquan was a Hakka from Guangdong who, after repeatedly failing the civil service examinations, came to believe through visions and Christian tracts that he was the younger brother of Jesus. He launched the Taiping Rebellion in 1850 and ruled the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom…

horacio-vasquez.s: Horacio Vásquez was a Dominican general and politician who served briefly as provisional president in 1899 and 1902–1903. Elected president in 1924, his victory ended the United States military occupation of the Dominican Republic.

house-of-barcelona.s: The House of Barcelona was the dynasty of counts of Barcelona descended from Wilfred the Hairy, who gathered several Catalan counties under one line in the late 9th century. By the marriage of Ramon Berenguer IV and Petronilla in 1137 it acquired the Kingdom of Aragon and…

house-of-reuss.s: The House of Reuss was a German noble family descended from the medieval Vögte of Weida, Gera and Plauen in eastern Thuringia, in which every male member was named Heinrich. Divided into an Elder and a Younger Line, it ruled several small counties and principalities,…

hrvoje-vukcic-hrvatinic.s: Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić was the most powerful Bosnian magnate of his day, who made and unmade Bosnian kings after the death of Tvrtko I. Backing Ladislaus of Naples against Sigismund for the Hungarian crown, he received the title Duke of Split and the central Dalmatian islands…

hussein-bin-ali-king-of-hejaz.n: Hussein bin Ali, King of Hejaz
hussein-bin-ali-king-of-hejaz.s: Hussein bin Ali, a Hashemite, was appointed Sharif and Emir of Mecca by the Ottomans in 1908. Encouraged by the Hussein–McMahon correspondence, he launched the Arab Revolt in June 1916 and proclaimed himself King of the Hejaz.

hue.s: Huế, formerly Phu Xuan, is a city on the Perfume River in central Vietnam. It became the seat of the Nguyen lords in the 17th and 18th centuries and was captured by the Tay Son.

house-of-saud.s: The House of Saud is the ruling family of Saudi Arabia, descended from Muhammad bin Saud, who became emir of Diriyah in 1727. His alliance with the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab in 1744 created the first Saudi state.

hieronymus-von-colloredo.s: Hieronymus von Colloredo was the last ruling prince-archbishop of Salzburg, elected in 1772. An enlightened reformer, he is best remembered as the employer of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, who left his service in 1781.

house-of-schwarzburg.s: The House of Schwarzburg was a Thuringian noble family, counts from the 12th century, whose lands lay around Schwarzburg, Arnstadt, Sondershausen and Rudolstadt. In 1349 Günther of Schwarzburg was elected German king against Charles IV, and on his withdrawal the family…

henry-v-the-fat.s: Henry V the Fat was a Silesian Piast duke of Legnica from 1278 and also of Wrocław from 1290. His reign was troubled by conflict with his cousin Henry III of Głogów, who held him captive for months.

henry-de-beaumont-1st-earl-of-warwick.n: Henry de Beaumont, 1st Earl of Warwick
henry-de-beaumont-1st-earl-of-warwick.s: Henry de Beaumont, 1st Earl of Warwick, was a Norman nobleman and companion of William II and Henry I of England. Around 1106 he took the Gower peninsula from its Welsh rulers, building a castle at Swansea and founding the marcher lordship of Gower.

henri-de-la-tour-dauvergne-duke-of-bouil.n: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon
henri-de-la-tour-dauvergne-duke-of-bouil.s: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon, was a French Huguenot noble, Viscount of Turenne and a Marshal of France from 1592. A companion of Henry IV, he married Charlotte de la Marck, heiress of Sedan and Bouillon, in 1591 and kept the principality after her death,…

haakon-vii.s: Haakon VII was King of Norway from 1905 to 1957, born Prince Carl of Denmark. After Norway dissolved its union with Sweden in 1905, a referendum confirmed him as king, and he took a traditional Norwegian royal name.

habibullah-kalakani.s: Habibullah Kalakani, nicknamed Bacha-i Saqao ('son of the water carrier'), was a Tajik rebel from the Shomali plain north of Kabul. Exploiting the revolts against King Amanullah Khan's reforms, he seized Kabul in January 1929 and ruled as emir for nine months.

hachisuka-iemasa.s: Hachisuka Iemasa was a Japanese daimyo, the son of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's retainer Hachisuka Masakatsu. After the conquest of Shikoku in 1585 Hideyoshi gave him Awa province, where he built Tokushima Castle.

hadadezer-of-zobah.s: Hadadezer son of Rehob was a king of Aram-Zobah, an Aramaean kingdom in the Beqaa valley and inland Syria, known from the Hebrew Bible. According to the books of Samuel and Chronicles he led a coalition of Aramaean states with chariots and forces reaching the Euphrates, but…

hadadezer-of-damascus.s: Hadadezer, called Adad-idri in Assyrian records, was a king of Aram-Damascus in the 9th century BCE. In 853 BCE he led a coalition including Irhuleni of Hamath and Ahab of Israel against Shalmaneser III of Assyria at the Battle of Qarqar, and he resisted further Assyrian…

hadiwijaya.s: Hadiwijaya, known in legend as Jaka Tingkir, was the founder and only significant ruler of the Pajang Sultanate in Central Java. A son-in-law of Sultan Trenggana of Demak, he defeated Arya Penangsang of Jipang with the help of Ratu Kalinyamat in the succession war after…

hafez-al-assad.s: Hafez al-Assad was a Syrian air force officer and Ba'ath party leader who seized power in 1970 and was President of Syria from 1971 until his death in 2000. He built a one-party state resting on the army, security services and his Alawite community, crushed the Hama uprising…

haitham-bin-tariq.s: Haitham bin Tariq is the Sultan of Oman, who succeeded his cousin Qaboos bin Said in January 2020. Before his accession he served as a senior diplomat, minister of heritage and culture and head of the Oman Vision 2040 committee.

haji-kerantukh-berzeg.s: Haji Kerantukh Berzeg was an Ubykh leader of the Berzeg family and one of the principal commanders of Circassian resistance to the Russian Empire. In 1861 he presided over the Circassian assembly at Sochi, which sought support from Britain and the Ottoman Empire.

haji-shah-of-yazd.s: Haji Shah was the last ruler of the Atabegs of Yazd, a local dynasty in central Iran under Ilkhanate overlordship. In 1319 he was defeated and driven out by Mubariz al-Din Muhammad, who took Yazd and made it the first base of the Muzaffarid dynasty, which later ruled Fars and…

hakon-grjotgardsson.s: Håkon Grjotgardsson was a Norwegian chieftain from Hålogaland in the late 9th century, the founder of the line of the Earls of Lade. According to the sagas he allied with Harald Fairhair during the unification of Norway and was made earl of Trøndelag.

halala-kella.s: Halala Kella is a long stone wall in the Dawro zone of south-western Ethiopia, running for well over 100 kilometres along the Omo river region. Tradition attributes it to King Halala of the Kingdom of Dawro, said to have been built to defend the realm against its neighbours,…

hamad-bin-abdullah-al-sharqi.s: Hamad bin Abdullah Al Sharqi was the chief of the Sharqiyin tribe of Fujairah on the east coast of the Arabian peninsula. In 1902 he asserted Fujairah's independence from the Qawasim of Sharjah, though Britain continued to regard it as part of Sharjah.

hamani-diori.s: Hamani Diori was the first President of Niger, from 1960 to 1974. A teacher and leader of the Niger Progressive Party, he was backed by France against Djibo Bakary's Sawaba party, which was banned after the 1958 referendum.

hamar-weyne.s: Hamar Weyne is one of the two oldest quarters of Mogadishu, on the coast of Somalia, alongside Shingani. Its narrow streets, coral-stone houses and mosques preserve the medieval core of the city, which grew rich on Indian Ocean trade.

hamid-ali-khan-of-rampur.s: Hamid Ali Khan was Nawab of Rampur from 1889 until his death in 1930. A patron of learning, music and Urdu poetry, he enlarged the Rampur Raza Library and built the Hamid Manzil palace that now houses it.

hamid-karzai.s: Hamid Karzai is a Pashtun politician of the Popalzai tribe who led Afghanistan after the fall of the Taliban regime in 2001. The Bonn Agreement made him head of the interim administration, and he was elected President of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan in 2004 and 2009,…

hamilcar-barca.s: Hamilcar Barca was a Carthaginian general who commanded in Sicily in the last years of the First Punic War and then crushed the Mercenary War in Africa. In 237 BCE he led an army to Iberia, where he conquered the Guadalquivir valley and its silver mines and founded a…

hammad-ibn-buluggin.s: Hammad ibn Buluggin was a Berber prince, son of the Zirid founder Buluggin ibn Ziri, who governed the western lands of the Zirid emirate in central Algeria. Around 1007 he founded the fortified city of Qal'at Beni Hammad in the Hodna mountains.

hamman-ruwa.s: Hamman Ruwa was a Fulani commander and the founder of the Muri Emirate in north-eastern Nigeria. A kinsman of Buba Yero of Gombe, he led Fulani forces south into the Benue valley in the jihad of the Sokoto Caliphate around 1817.

hammuda-pasha-bey.s: Hammuda Pasha Bey was the second bey of the Muradid dynasty of Ottoman Tunisia, ruling from 1631 to 1666. Son of Murad I Bey, he received the title of pasha from the Ottoman sultan and made the office of bey hereditary in his family, overshadowing the dey.

hammurabi-of-kurda.s: Hammurabi of Kurda was a king of Kurda, a small state in northern Mesopotamia, in the 18th century BCE, a contemporary of his more famous namesake of Babylon. He is known from the Mari letters, which show him making and breaking alliances with Mari, Andarig, Eshnunna and…

handsome-lake.s: Handsome Lake was a Seneca prophet and chief, half-brother of Cornplanter. After a series of visions in 1799, he preached the Gaiwiio ('Good Message'), which called for temperance, a return to traditional ceremonies and adaptation to farming and family life.

hans-adam-dorten.s: Hans Adam Dorten was a German lawyer and Rhineland separatist leader. With French encouragement he proclaimed a Rhenish Republic at Wiesbaden in June 1919, which collapsed within days, and he again led the separatist movement during the occupation of the Ruhr in 1923.

hans-egede.s: Hans Egede was a Norwegian Lutheran missionary who sailed to Greenland in 1721 hoping to find the descendants of the medieval Norse settlers. Finding only Inuit, he founded a mission and trading post at Godthåb (Nuuk) in 1728 and learned their language.

hans-waldmann.s: Hans Waldmann was a Swiss military commander and Mayor of Zürich from 1483. He fought with distinction against Charles the Bold of Burgundy, notably at Morat in 1476, and made Zürich a leading power in the Swiss Confederacy.

haqqi-al-azm.s: Haqqi al-Azm was a Syrian politician from the prominent Azm family of Damascus and a supporter of cooperation with France. He was appointed first governor of the State of Damascus under the French Mandate in 1920, and he later served as Prime Minister of Syria from 1932 to…

harald-bluetooth.s: Harald Bluetooth was King of Denmark from about 958 to about 986, the son of Gorm the Old. He accepted Christianity around 965 and raised the larger Jelling Stone, which claims that he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.

hari-singh.s: Hari Singh was the last Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir, reigning from 1925 to 1952. At the partition of India in 1947 he hesitated between India and Pakistan, hoping for independence.

hari-singh-vidyadhar.s: Hari Singh Vidyadhar was a military commander of the Gajapati Kingdom of Odisha who, according to tradition, defeated a local chief named Dhenka and founded the state of Dhenkanal in 1529. The town and state took their name from the defeated chief.

harinder-singh-brar.s: Harinder Singh Brar was the last ruling Raja of Faridkot, a Sikh princely state in the Punjab, from 1918, governing in person from 1934. He acceded to India in 1947, and in 1948 Faridkot was merged into the Patiala and East Punjab States Union.

harold-ingrams.s: Harold Ingrams was a British colonial officer who served in Zanzibar and Mauritius before becoming political officer in the Hadhramaut in southern Arabia. In 1937 he negotiated a truce among hundreds of feuding tribes and towns, known as Ingrams' Peace, which brought security…

harsha.s: Harsha, or Harshavardhana, was the most famous ruler of the Pushyabhuti dynasty, reigning from 606 to 647 from Thanesar and Kannauj over much of northern India. A patron of Buddhism and letters, he wrote three Sanskrit plays and was described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang…

harsha-of-kashmir.s: Harsha was a king of Kashmir of the Lohara dynasty, reigning from 1089 to 1101. A cultured ruler and poet, he later turned to heavy taxation and melted down temple images to pay his troops, conflicts recorded in Kalhana's Rajatarangini.

hasan-al-kalbi.s: Hasan al-Kalbi was the first emir of Sicily of the Kalbid dynasty, appointed by the Fatimid caliph al-Mansur in 948 to restore order on the island. He suppressed revolts in Palermo, fought the Byzantines in Calabria and founded a hereditary line that ruled Sicily under Fatimid…

hasan-al-utrush.s: Hasan al-Utrush, called al-Nasir al-Kabir, was a Zaydi imam and Alid ruler in Tabaristan on the Caspian coast of Iran. He converted many Daylamites and Gilites to Zaydi Islam and in 914 restored the Alavid state after its fall to the Samanids.

hasan-buzurg.s: Hasan Buzurg ('Hasan the Tall') was a Mongol emir of the Jalayir tribe and founder of the Jalayirid dynasty. After the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id died in 1335, he raised puppet khans and fought the Chupanids for control of the Ilkhanate's heartlands, securing Baghdad and Iraq by 1340.

hasan-ii-of-alamut.s: Hasan II was the fourth ruler of the Nizari Ismaili state of Alamut in northern Iran, from 1162 to 1166. In 1164 he proclaimed the qiyama, the spiritual resurrection, abrogating the outward rules of Islamic law for his followers, and he was recognised as imam.

hasan-pasha-of-baghdad.s: Hasan Pasha was an Ottoman governor of Baghdad from 1704 until his death in 1723. He and his son Ahmad Pasha, who succeeded him, built up a household of slave soldiers, mostly from Georgia, trained for war and administration.

hasan-jalal-dawla.s: Hasan-Jalal Dawla was the Armenian prince of Khachen, in present-day Karabakh, from 1214 until his death in 1261. He built the monastery of Gandzasar, seat of the Catholicos of Aghvank, consecrated in 1240.

hasanwayh-ibn-husayn.s: Hasanwayh ibn Husayn was a chief of the Kurdish Barzikani tribe who founded the Hasanwayhid dynasty in the western Zagros. From 959 he ruled the mountains around Dinavar, Hamadan, Nahavand and Shahrizor under the loose overlordship of the Buyids.

hashim-ibn-suraqa.s: Hashim ibn Suraqa was an Arab governor of Derbent on the Caspian coast of the Caucasus who in 869, as Abbasid authority weakened, founded the hereditary Hashimid dynasty. Under his line Derbent became an independent frontier emirate, waging holy war against the peoples of the…

hassan-ali-bayoomi.s: Hassan Ali Bayoomi was an Aden politician and journalist who served as chief minister of the colony and then of the State of Aden in 1963. He supported Aden's merger into the British-backed Federation of South Arabia, against the opposition of nationalists and trade unions.

hassan-ii-of-morocco.s: Hassan II was King of Morocco from 1961 until his death in 1999, of the Alaouite dynasty. He introduced constitutions but kept firm power, surviving military coup attempts in 1971 and 1972 and repressing opponents during the period known as the Years of Lead.

hastings-banda.s: Hastings Kamuzu Banda was a Malawian physician and politician who led Nyasaland to independence as Malawi in 1964. He returned home in 1958 to lead the campaign against the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland and was detained during the 1959 emergency.

haydar-khan-amu-oghli.s: Haydar Khan Amu-oghli was an Iranian revolutionary who took part in the Persian Constitutional Revolution and later led the Communist Party of Iran. In 1921 he was sent to Gilan to reconcile the communists with Mirza Kuchik Khan's Jangali movement in the Persian Socialist…

haydar-quli-khan.s: Haydar Quli Khan was a chief of the Turkic Kangarlu tribe who declared himself khan of Nakhichevan after the death of Nader Shah in 1747. He founded the Nakhichevan Khanate, which his family ruled under shifting Persian overlordship until it was ceded to Russia by the Treaty…

hazael.s: Hazael was a king of Aram-Damascus who seized the throne around 842 BCE; an Assyrian text calls him the son of a nobody. He resisted Shalmaneser III of Assyria and then dominated the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, conquering lands east of the Jordan and destroying Gath.

hazael-of-qedar.s: Hazael was a king of the Qedarite Arabs of northern Arabia in the early 7th century BCE. Sennacherib of Assyria seized the images of his gods at Adummatu (Dumat al-Jandal), which Esarhaddon later returned after Hazael submitted.

heden-ii.s: Heden II was a duke of Thuringia of the Hedenid line, based at Würzburg on the Main, in the early 8th century. He supported the Anglo-Saxon missionary Willibrord, granting him estates at Arnstadt in 704, and a church was founded on the Marienberg at Würzburg.

heinrich-toppler.s: Heinrich Toppler was Mayor of Rothenburg ob der Tauber in Franconia several times between 1373 and 1407. Under his leadership the imperial city bought up a large rural territory and fought neighbouring lords.

heinrich-von-plauen.s: Heinrich von Plauen was a knight of the Teutonic Order from the family of the reeves of Plauen in the Vogtland. After the order's defeat at Grunwald in 1410 he organised the successful defence of Marienburg against Poland-Lithuania, and he was elected Grand Master.

heinrich-x-reuss-of-lobenstein.s: Heinrich X was a count of the Younger Line of the House of Reuss, which named all its male members Heinrich. In the division of 1647 he received Lobenstein in the Thuringian Highlands, founding the line of Reuss-Lobenstein.

heinrich-x-reuss-of-ebersdorf.s: Heinrich X was a younger son of the Lobenstein line of the House of Reuss, for whom the small county of Reuss-Ebersdorf in the Thuringian Highlands was separated in 1678. He and his wife Erdmuthe Benigna made Ebersdorf a centre of Pietism.

heinrich-xi-prince-reuss-of-greiz.n: Heinrich XI, Prince Reuss of Greiz
heinrich-xi-prince-reuss-of-greiz.s: Heinrich XI was a count of the Elder Line of the House of Reuss who reunited Upper and Lower Greiz in 1768. In 1778 he was raised to the rank of prince of the Holy Roman Empire, making Reuss-Greiz a principality.

helian-chang.s: Helian Chang was the second emperor of the Xiongnu-led Helian Xia state in northern China, succeeding his father Helian Bobo in 425. Northern Wei forces took the capital Tongwan in 427 and captured him in 428.

helian-ding.s: Helian Ding was the last emperor of Helian Xia, the brother of Helian Chang, who rallied the remnants of the state after Chang's capture by Northern Wei in 428. In 431 he destroyed the Western Qin kingdom, but while crossing the Yellow River he was captured by the Tuyuhun, who…

helmut-kohl.s: Helmut Kohl was a German Christian Democratic politician who was Chancellor of West Germany and then of reunified Germany from 1982 to 1998, the longest-serving chancellor since Bismarck. After the fall of the Berlin Wall he pushed rapidly for reunification, achieved on 3…
